theme: Kings condemned; the good and bad figs; the 70 years
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 21:1-24:10. Jeremiah speaks to the last kings of Judah, promises a righteous Branch, condemns the false shepherds, and sees two baskets of figs. Read 23:1-8 and chapter 24 slowly.
settingTheScene: These chapters mostly date to the reign of Zedekiah, the last king, around 590 BC, while Babylon was closing in. The king sends messengers to Jeremiah asking for a miracle, and the prophet answers that God himself is fighting against Jerusalem. Then he describes the failure of the kings of Judah. In the midst of the gloom come some of the book’s most important promises of a coming king and a restored remnant.
observation: “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death” (21:8).
“Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness… who makes his neighbor serve him for nothing” (22:13).
“Did not your father eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? … He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me?” (22:15-16).
“Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” (23:1).
“Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch” (23:5).
“And this is the name by which he will be called: The LORD is our righteousness” (23:6).
“Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away?” (23:23).
“Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah” (24:5).
interpretation:
The king asks for a miracle, as Hezekiah once received. But this time there is no deliverance. God says, “I myself will fight against you.” The choice for the people is stark: go out and surrender to Babylon and live, or stay and die. It sounds like treason, and Jeremiah is treated that way. It was actually a call to humble submission to God’s chastening.

Chapters 22 and 23 deal with the kings. Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Jehoiachin are in turn condemned. Jehoiakim built a luxurious palace with forced labor. God contrasts him with his father Josiah, who did justice and righteousness and judged the cause of the poor and needy. The key line: “Is not this to know me?” To know God is to care for the vulnerable. Knowledge of God is shown in justice.

Then the shepherds. God accuses the leaders of scattering his flock. But he will gather the remnant himself and give them shepherds who will feed them. And then the promise: “I will raise up for David a righteous Branch.” This king will reign wisely and do justice. His name is “The LORD is our righteousness.” Zedekiah means “The LORD is my righteousness,” but the last king of Judah did not live up to his name. The Branch will.

The chapter then attacks the false prophets who speak visions of their own minds and say, “It shall be well with you.” They have not stood in the council of the LORD. God’s word is like fire and like a hammer.

Chapter 24 gives a vision of two baskets of figs: good figs and bad. The surprise is who is who. The good figs are the exiles in Babylon, and the bad figs are those left in Jerusalem. God says the exiles are his remnant: “I will build them up, and not tear down.” “I will give them a heart to know that I am the LORD.” What looks like judgment is the path to new life.
connection: Matthew 1:21 gives the name Jesus: he will save his people. 1 Corinthians 1:30 says Christ became for us righteousness. Ezekiel 34 develops the shepherd image, and Jesus fulfills it in John 10:11. Matthew 7:15-20 warns about false prophets who are known by their fruit. Philippians 2:12-13 says God works in us to will and to do his good pleasure. Romans 8:28 says that God works all things for good.
application:
Ask whether your knowledge of God is shown in how you treat the poor and needy, as Jeremiah says it should be.

Pray for church leaders to be faithful shepherds, and for your own shepherding of those in your care.

Consider a season in your life that seemed like exile. How did God use it to give you a heart to know him?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is our righteousness.
Thank him for the righteous Branch of David.
Ask him to give his people shepherds after his own heart.
